title: The Verb 'To Be' (Bi)
body: Scottish Gaelic has two 'to be' verbs: 'is' and 'bi'. 'Bi' is used for states and ongoing actions. Present tense: tha mi (I am), chan eil mi (I am not), a bheil thu? (are you?). Past: bha mi (I was). Future: bidh mi (I will be).

examples.en: I am tired.
You are not right.
Is she happy?

title: Verbal Nouns (the '-ing' form)
body: Gaelic expresses continuous action with 'tha' + subject + 'a/ag' + verbal noun, similar to English '-ing'. E.g. 'a' bruidhinn' (speaking), 'ag ithe' (eating). The particle is 'ag' before a vowel and 'a'' before a consonant.

examples.en: I am eating.
She is speaking.

title: Lenition (Initial Consonant Mutation)
body: Many Gaelic words change their first letter (lenition, adding an 'h') in certain grammatical contexts, e.g. after 'mo' (my) or feminine nouns after 'an' (the). 'Mathair' becomes 'mo mhàthair' (my mother). This is one of the trickiest parts of Gaelic grammar for beginners — recognise it rather than memorise every rule at first.

examples.en: mother -> my mother
small -> my small (one)

title: Questions and Negatives with 'Bi'
body: Unlike English, Gaelic doesn't use a separate 'do' for questions. The verb itself changes form: 'tha' (statement) -> 'a bheil?' (question) -> 'chan eil' (negative). This pattern recurs with other irregular verbs too, each with its own question/negative form.

examples.en: You are tired.
Are you tired?
You are not tired.

title: Basic Word Order (VSO)
body: Gaelic sentences normally start with the verb, then the subject, then the object (Verb-Subject-Object), unlike English's Subject-Verb-Object. 'Tha mi sgìth' is literally 'Am I tired' in word order, meaning 'I am tired'.

examples.en: I saw the cat. (lit: Saw I the cat)

title: The Past Tense of Regular Verbs
body: Most regular verbs form the past tense by lenition of the root alone (no extra word needed), and add 'do' optionally before vowels. 'Bruidhinn' (to speak) -> 'bhruidhinn mi' (I spoke). The question form uses 'an do...?' and the negative uses 'cha do...'.

examples.en: I spoke to him yesterday.
Did you speak to him?
I did not speak to him.

title: Prepositional Pronouns
body: Gaelic fuses common prepositions with pronouns into single words, e.g. 'aig' (at) + mi -> 'agam' (at me / I have), 'air' (on) + i -> 'oirre' (on her). These are essential for expressing possession and many everyday phrases, and must be learned as whole forms rather than built on the fly.

examples.en: I have a dog. (lit: there is a dog at-me)
I am hungry. (lit: the hunger is on-me)

title: Comparatives and Superlatives
body: To compare adjectives, Gaelic typically uses 'nas' + a modified ('comparative') form of the adjective, and 'as' in relative clauses for superlatives. 'Math' (good) becomes 'nas fheàrr' (better) and 'as fheàrr' (best) — many common adjectives are irregular, similar to English 'good/better/best'.

examples.gd: Tha seo nas fheàrr na sin.
examples.en: This is better than that.

examples.gd: Is e seo an rud as fheàrr.
examples.en: This is the best thing.

title: Talking About Liking Things
body: 'To like' is expressed indirectly: 'is toil leam' (lit. 'it is pleasing with me'). The negative is 'cha toil leam', and 'is fheàrr leam' means 'I prefer'. The verbal noun follows directly.

examples.gd: Is toil leam a bhith a' leughadh.
examples.en: I like reading.
I don't like coffee.

examples.gd: Is fheàrr leam tì na cofaidh.
examples.en: I prefer tea to coffee.

title: Relative Clauses (a/nach)
body: Gaelic uses the particle 'a' (lenites the verb) to form relative clauses like English 'who/that/which', and 'nach' for the negative form. The verb form also changes depending on whether the relative clause is direct or indirect, which takes practice to internalise.

examples.en: The man whom I saw
The thing that is not right

title: The Conditional Mood
body: To express 'would' Gaelic uses the conditional, formed with lenition and often ending in '-adh/-eadh' for regular verbs: 'dh'òlainn' (I would drink). Irregular verbs like 'bi' have their own conditional ('bhithinn' — I would be).

examples.gd: Dh'òlainn cupa tì, mas e do thoil e.
examples.en: I would drink a cup of tea, please.

examples.gd: Nam biodh an t-airgead agam, cheannaichinn taigh.
examples.en: If I had the money, I would buy a house.

title: Conditional Sentences with 'Nam'
body: Hypothetical 'if' clauses use 'nam' (if, for hypothetical/unreal conditions) with the conditional/dependent form of the verb, contrasted with 'ma' which is used for real/possible conditions with the present or future tense.

examples.gd: Ma tha thu sgìth, gabh fois.
examples.en: If you are tired, rest. (real condition)

examples.gd: Nam bithinn beairteach, shiubhlainn an saoghal.
examples.en: If I were rich, I would travel the world. (hypothetical)

title: The Passive-like 'Rach' Construction
body: Gaelic often expresses passive meaning with 'rach' (to go) + the verbal noun with 'a dhèanamh' pattern, roughly 'get done'. This is more common than a true grammatical passive in everyday Gaelic.

examples.gd: Chaidh an taigh a thogail an-uiridh.
examples.en: The house was built last year. (lit: went the house to-building)

examples.gd: Thèid am biadh a dheasachadh a-nis.
examples.en: The food will be prepared now.

title: Connecting Ideas: Subordinate Clauses
body: Beyond simple sentences, B1 Gaelic relies on connectors like 'oir' (because), 'ged a' (although), 'mus' (before), and 'nuair a' (when) to build more complex, multi-clause sentences — essential for narrating events and giving reasons.

examples.gd: Dh'fhan mi aig an taigh oir bha an t-uisge ann.
examples.en: I stayed home because it was raining.

examples.gd: Ged a bha mi sgìth, chaidh mi a-mach.
examples.en: Although I was tired, I went out.

title: Reported Speech
body: Reporting what someone said shifts tense and pronouns similarly to English, usually introduced by 'thuirt e/i gu(n)/gu robh...' (he/she said that...). 'Gu' triggers a dependent verb form, and negative reported clauses use 'nach'.

examples.gd: Thuirt i gun robh i sgìth.
examples.en: She said that she was tired.

examples.gd: Thuirt e nach robh e airson tighinn.
examples.en: He said that he didn't want to come.

title: Impersonal and Autonomous Verb Forms
body: Gaelic has a distinct 'autonomous' verb form (no stated subject) used heavily in formal, news, and narrative registers, roughly equivalent to English passive or 'one does X'. It typically ends in '-ar' (present/future) or '-adh' (past), e.g. 'nithear' (it is done / one does).

examples.en: It is being said that... (impersonal)

examples.gd: Chaidh aithris gun deach an aonta a shoidhnigeadh.
examples.en: It was reported that the agreement was signed.

title: Register and Idiomatic Connectors
body: At B2, fluent-sounding Gaelic depends less on new grammar rules and more on idiomatic discourse markers used in debate, news, and essay-style writing: 'a rèir choltais' (apparently), 'air an làimh eile' (on the other hand), 'aig a' cheann thall' (ultimately). Learning to deploy these naturally is what separates B1 from B2 fluency.

examples.gd: Air an làimh eile, tha buannachdan ann cuideachd.
examples.en: On the other hand, there are advantages too.

examples.gd: Aig a' cheann thall, 's e co-dhùnadh a' choimhearsnachd a bhios cudromach.
examples.en: Ultimately, the community's decision will be what matters.

title: Formal Written Style and Nominalisation
body: Formal and written Gaelic (news, policy, essays) favours turning verbs into abstract nouns ('nominalisation'), much like English 'implementation' instead of 'to implement'. Recognising and using forms like 'buileachadh' (implementation, from 'builich') is key to reading and writing at B2.

examples.gd: Tha am buileachadh a' tòiseachadh an ath-bhliadhna.
examples.en: The implementation starts next year.
There was controversy about the new policy.

title: The Ten Irregular Verbs
body: Almost every Gaelic course front-loads the same ten irregular verbs, because they don't follow the regular lenition pattern for the past tense and have unique verbal nouns: bi (be), abair (say) -> ag ràdh, beir (bear/catch) -> a' breith, cluinn (hear) -> a' cluinntinn, dèan (do/make) -> a' dèanamh, faic (see) -> a' faicinn, faigh (get) -> a' faighinn, rach (go) -> a' dol, ith (eat) -> ag ithe, thig (come) -> a' tighinn, thoir (give) -> a' toirt. Learn each pair (infinitive + verbal noun) together rather than trying to derive one from the other.

examples.en: I went to the shop. (rach, irregular past)
She gave me a book. (thoir, irregular past)

title: Past and Future of the Irregular Verbs
body: Each of the ten irregular verbs has its own past and future stem instead of following the regular lenition/no-change pattern. Worth drilling as fixed forms: rach -> chaidh mi (I went) / thèid mi (I will go); faigh -> fhuair mi (I got) / gheibh mi (I will get); dèan -> rinn mi (I did) / nì mi (I will do); abair -> thuirt mi (I said) / canaidh mi (I will say); thoir -> thug mi (I gave) / bheir mi (I will give).

examples.en: I got a letter yesterday.
I will do that tomorrow.

examples.gd: Thuirt i gun canadh i rium.
examples.en: She said she would tell me. (canaidh -> canadh in reported/conditional form)

title: The Imperative Mood
body: Commands and requests use the imperative, usually the bare verb root for 'you' singular/informal, with 'ibh' added for plural/formal: 'bruidhinn' (speak!) vs 'bruidhnibh' (speak!, pl./formal). Negative commands use 'na': 'na bruidhinn' (don't speak!).

examples.gd: Fosgail an doras, mas e do thoil e.
examples.en: Open the door, please.
Don't be late!

title: Indirect (Embedded) Questions
body: When a question is embedded inside another sentence ('I don't know where he is' rather than 'Where is he?'), Gaelic keeps the dependent form of the verb and the question word, introduced by a linking particle similar to 'gu/an' patterns used for reported speech.

examples.gd: Chan eil fhios agam càite a bheil e.
examples.en: I don't know where he is.

examples.gd: Dh'fhaighnich i dè bha mi a' dèanamh.
examples.en: She asked what I was doing.

title: The Emphatic Copula: 'Is e ... a tha'
body: To emphasise or contrast who/what something is, Gaelic fronts the emphasised item with the copula 'is' plus 'e/i' and a relative clause, roughly 'it is X that...'. This cleft-sentence pattern is extremely common in B2-level argumentation and formal speech for highlighting a specific point.

examples.gd: Is e an fhianais a tha cudromach, chan e am beachd.
examples.en: It's the evidence that matters, not the opinion.

examples.gd: Is e sin as coireach ris an duilgheadas.
examples.en: That is what is causing the problem.

title: Emphatic Pronouns
body: Gaelic has a separate set of emphatic pronoun forms used to stress contrast ('I did, not you'): mise (I/me, emphatic), thusa (you, emphatic), esan (he/him, emphatic), ise (she/her, emphatic), sinne (we/us, emphatic), sibhse (you pl., emphatic), iadsan (they/them, emphatic). These appear constantly in natural debate/conversation at B2 and above.

examples.gd: Rinn mise sin, chan e thusa.
examples.en: I did that, not you.
They were there too.

title: Comparative Subordinate Clauses
body: Beyond the simple 'nas fheàrr na' (better than) comparative from A2, B2 Gaelic builds fuller comparative clauses with a verb on both sides, often using 'na bha dùil' (than expected) or 'mar a bha' (as it was) patterns, and 'a cheart cho... ri' (just as... as) for equal comparisons. These let you compare actions and whole situations, not just two nouns.

examples.gd: Bha am buaidh na bu mhotha na bha dùil againn.
examples.en: The impact was greater than we expected.

examples.gd: Tha an suidheachadh a cheart cho duilich ri mar a bha e an-uiridh.
examples.en: The situation is just as difficult as it was last year.

examples.gd: Mar as motha a dh'ionnsaicheas tu, 's ann as fhasa a bhios e.
examples.en: The more you learn, the easier it becomes. (correlative comparative)

title: Possessive Pronouns (mo, do, a, ar, ur, an/am)
body: Gaelic possessives ('my', 'your', 'his'...) go before the noun and several of them trigger lenition on the word that follows: mo (my) and do (your, informal) lenite; a (his) lenites; a (her) does not lenite but adds an 'h' before a vowel instead; ar (our), ur (your, formal/plural) and an/am (their) don't lenite. Learn each possessive together with whether it lenites, rather than as a single uniform rule.

examples.en: my brother

examples.gd: a bràthair (her brother, no lenition) vs a bhràthair (his brother, lenited)
examples.en: her brother / his brother — same spelling pattern 'a', opposite lenition
our family

title: 'Fhìn' — the Reflexive/Emphatic 'Self'
body: Adding 'fhìn' after a pronoun means 'self' (myself, yourself...) and is commonly used to turn a question back on someone, similar to English 'and you?' after answering 'how are you?'. Don't confuse this with the separate emphatic pronoun set (mise, thusa, esan...) from g024 — 'fhìn' adds emphasis/reflexivity to the normal pronoun, it doesn't replace it.

examples.gd: Tha mi gu math, tapadh leat. Ciamar a tha thu fhìn?
examples.en: I'm fine, thanks. How about you(rself)?
I did that myself.

title: The Definite Article: an, am, an t-, a', na, na h-
body: Gaelic has no word for 'a/an' (nouns just stand alone), but 'the' changes shape depending on the noun's gender and first letter. Most nouns use 'an'. Masculine nouns starting with a 'lip' sound (b/f/m/p) use 'am' instead. Masculine nouns starting with a vowel use 'an t-'. Feminine nouns starting with b/c/g/m/p use 'a'' plus lenition; feminine nouns starting with 's' followed by l/n/r/a vowel also take 'an t-' (not 'a''), e.g. 'an t-seanmhair' (the grandmother). The plural 'the' is 'na' (or 'na h-' before a vowel). It looks like a lot of forms, but they all follow from gender + first letter, so learn the pattern rather than each word's article by heart.

examples.en: the table (masculine, starts with b)
the water/rain (masculine, starts with a vowel)
the old woman (feminine, starts with c, lenited)
the nose (feminine, starts with s+vowel, takes an t- not a')
the houses / the eggs (plural, consonant vs vowel)

title: More Lenition Triggers (glè, ro, aon, dà, gun, cha)
body: Beyond possessives (g026), several other very common words trigger lenition on the word right after them: 'glè' (very), 'ro' (too), 'aon' (one), 'dà' (two), 'gun' (without) and the negative 'cha' (not). A few consonant clusters are immune to lenition no matter what precedes them: 'sg', 'sp', 'sm' and 'st' never lenite, and words starting with d/s/t often resist lenition after 'aon', 'gun' and 'cha' specifically (e.g. 'cha tig', not 'cha dhig').

examples.en: very small (beag -> bheag)
two houses (taigh -> thaigh)

examples.gd: cha bhi mi ann, ach cha tig thu.
examples.en: I won't be there, but you won't come. (bi lenites, tig resists after cha)

title: Adjectives That Go Before the Noun
body: Almost all Gaelic adjectives follow the noun they describe (taigh mòr, a big house), but a small, fixed set goes in front instead, the way English always does: 'deagh' (good), 'droch' (bad), 'seann' (old) and 'fìor' (genuine/true). These front-position adjectives also typically lenite the noun that follows.

examples.en: a good day
bad weather
an old car
a genuine/real man

title: Irregular Comparatives and the Past-Tense 'Bu'
body: Many common adjectives have an irregular comparative/superlative stem instead of the regular 'slenderise + e' pattern: math (good) -> nas fheàrr/as fheàrr; mòr (big) -> nas motha/as motha; beag (small) -> nas lugha/as lugha; dona (bad) -> nas miosa/as miosa. To compare things in the past tense, 'nas'/'as' are replaced by 'bu'/'b'' (lenites a following consonant): 'bu bhrèagha' (was more beautiful), 'b'e Iain a b'òige' (Iain was the youngest).

examples.gd: Tha seo nas fheàrr na sin.
examples.en: This is better than that. (present)

examples.gd: Bha i na bu bhrèagha na Anna.
examples.en: She was more beautiful than Anna. (past)

title: Root vs Verbal Noun: How a Gaelic Verb Is Built
body: Every Gaelic verb has two core citation forms you'll meet constantly: the 'root' (the bare command form, and the base the past/future/conditional are built from) and the 'verbal noun' (used after 'tha...a'/ag' for ongoing action, and after 'a'/a dh'' for the infinitive 'to do X'). Dictionaries list both. 'Seas' (stand) is the root; 'seasamh' is its verbal noun, giving 'tha mi a' seasamh' (I am standing) and 'a sheasamh' (to stand).

examples.en: put -> putting (an irregular-looking but common pair)

examples.gd: Tha mi a' dol a dh'òl.
examples.en: I am going to drink. (a dh' before a vowel-initial verbal noun)

title: Regular Past Tense: the Full Pattern
body: Building on g006, the regular past tense actually splits three ways depending on the root's first letter. Lenite the root if it starts with b/c/d/g/m/p/t, or with f+consonant/s+vowel: buail -> bhuail (hit/hit). Leave it unchanged if it starts with l/n/r or sg/sm/sp/st: stad -> stad (stop/stopped) — identical to the root. Add 'dh'' in front if it starts with a vowel or f+vowel: òl -> dh'òl (drink/drank), feuch -> dh'fheuch (try/tried, the f stays silent).

examples.en: He lay down on the floor. (laigh is unchanged — starts with l)
I rose early. (vowel-initial root gets dh')

title: Prepositional Possessives (gam, nam, gad, nad...)
body: When a possessive ('my', 'your'...) combines with the prepositions 'aig' (at) or 'ann' (in), the two fuse into a single short word: aig+mo -> gam, ann+mo -> nam, aig+do -> gad, ann+do -> nad, and so on for each person. These are common in set phrases about ongoing states and feelings ('tha X gam...' patterns) and are worth recognising as a fused pair rather than puzzling over which preposition and possessive they came from.

examples.en: She is helping me. (aig + mo -> gam)

examples.gd: Tha an leabhar agam nam phòcaid.
examples.en: My book is in my pocket. (ann + mo -> nam)

title: Noun Cases: Nominative, Vocative, Dative, Genitive
body: Gaelic nouns change their spelling slightly depending on their grammatical role, a system of four 'cases'. Nominative is the plain form (subject of a sentence). Vocative is used when addressing someone directly, marked by 'a' plus lenition (and slenderising for masculine names): 'a Mhàiri!', 'a Dhòmhnaill!'. Dative follows simple prepositions like 'ann'/'air'/'do' and often slenderises a feminine noun's final vowel. Genitive marks possession/'of' relationships and follows compound prepositions, often changing the noun's ending (e.g. 'obair-sgoile', schoolwork). You don't need to memorise full declension tables to get by, but recognising *why* a word's ending shifted helps a lot when reading.

examples.en: James! (vocative, lenited + slenderised)
in the town (dative, after a simple preposition)
the dog's leg (genitive, 'of the dog')

title: Demonstratives: seo, sin, siud
body: Gaelic has three degrees of 'this/that' based on distance from the speaker, not just two like English: 'seo' (this, near), 'sin' (that, middle distance — the most commonly used of the three), and 'siud'/'ud' (that yonder, far away or out of sight). Each also has pronoun and adverb forms: 'an seo' (here), 'an sin' (there), 'an siud' (yonder).

examples.en: Here is the little boy. (seo, near)
That's not right. (sin, middle — the default 'that')
Who is that over there? (siud, far/out of sight)

title: Prepositional Pronouns with 'Do' and 'Le'
body: Two more common prepositions fuse with pronouns the same way 'aig' and 'air' do (g007). 'Do' (to) gives: dhomh (to me), dhut (to you), dha (to him), dhi (to her), dhuinn (to us), dhuibh (to you pl.), dhaibh (to them) — heard constantly in greetings like 'oidhche mhath dhut'. 'Le' (with) gives: leam, leat, leis, leatha, leinn, leibh, leotha, and builds the common phrases 'is toil leam' (I like) and 'is fheàrr leam' (I prefer) you already know from g009.

examples.en: Good afternoon to you! (formal/plural)
Goodbye. (lit. 'a blessing with you')
Who does this belong to? (lit. 'with whom is this')

title: Numbers with Nouns: Singular, Dual, and Lenition
body: Counting a noun in Gaelic doesn't just stick a plural on after 3+ the way English does. 'Aon' (one) and 'dà' (two) are both followed by the *singular* form of the noun, not the plural — this is sometimes called the 'dual'. Plural only kicks in from 'trì' (three) onward. 'Aon' and 'dà' also lenite the noun that follows, except 'aon' doesn't lenite nouns starting with d or t.

examples.gd: aon chat, dà chupa, trì balaich
examples.en: one cat, two cups, three boys (singular, singular, then plural)
one house — 'aon' skips lenition before t/d

title: Expressing Profession or Temporary State with 'Na' + Possessive
body: A very common way to say what someone's job is, or to describe a temporary state, uses 'ann' fused with a possessive (nam/nad/na/na/nar/nur/nan — the same fusion family as g034) placed between 'tha' and the noun: literally 'I am in-my teacher'. Masculine 'na' lenites the following noun, feminine 'na' does not — the same his/her asymmetry as other possessives. The same pattern covers everyday idioms like being alone, asleep, or in a hurry, not just professions.

examples.en: He is a teacher. (masculine na, lenited)
She is a teacher. (feminine na, not lenited)
I am alone.
They are asleep.

title: Static vs Motion Direction Words (shuas/suas, shios/sios...)
body: Several Gaelic direction words come in pairs: one form for a fixed location, another for movement toward it — a distinction English doesn't mark. 'Shuas' (up, a place) vs 'suas' (upwards, movement); 'shios' (down, a place) vs 'sios' (downwards, movement); 'a-muigh' (outside, a place) vs 'a-mach' (out, movement); 'a-staigh' (inside, a place) vs 'a-steach' (in, movement). Picking the wrong one of the pair is a very common learner mix-up, so it's worth drilling as pairs rather than learning each word alone.

examples.en: He is upstairs. (shuas, static location)

examples.gd: Tha e a' dol suas an staidhre.
examples.en: He is going upstairs. (suas, movement)
She is outside. (static)
She is going out. (movement)
